pamphlet_excerpts: Hazards, First Aid & Safety: Even a gentle sport like fly-fishing can come with its perils (p. 77).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 2: Agood angler will be well-versed in first-aid for cuts, scratches, puncture wounds, and insect bites and stings (p. 77).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 3: Cuts and scratches are wounds, openings in the skin and tissues that can allow germs to enter the body and causeinfection (p. 77).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 4: Wash minor scratches and cuts with soap and water (p. 77).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): On camping trips, clean and rebandage small wounds daily (p. 77).
Step 2 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Larger cuts should be treated with direct pressure to stopbleeding, then cleaned as well as possible to limit infection (p. 77).
Step 3 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Cover an open wound with a sterile gauze pad or clean cloth that has been folded to make a pad (p. 77).
Step 4 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Hold the pad in position with tape, a cravat bandage, or other binder (p. 77).

pamphlet_excerpts: Match A Fly Rod Line: Lines vary by weight, and must be matched to the rod (p. 13).
Match A Fly Rod Line Principle 2: They come in different styles (called tapers) and colors and are designed either to float on the surface of the water or to sink to different depths (p. 13).
Match A Fly Rod Line Principle 3: Intermediate lines, for example, sink very slowly and can be fished just below the surface (p. 13).
Match A Fly Rod Line Principle 4: Heavily weighted lines sinkquite rapidly and are designed to get down deep very quickly (p. 13).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Match A Fly Rod Line): Most fly-fishing is done with floating lines, which are the easiest to cast and control (p. 13).
Step 2 (Match A Fly Rod Line): But there are times and conditions whenfish lie deeply in the water and are not feeding at or near the surface (p. 13).
Step 3 (Match A Fly Rod Line): A sinking line is then useful to get the fly down to them (p. 13).
Step 4 (Match A Fly Rod Line): Sinking lines usuallycome in drab, darker colors so that the fish cannot spot them (p. 13).

pamphlet_excerpts: Essential Fly-Fishing Knots and Leaders: Use these flies to catch trout, bass andpanfish on the water's surface (p. 38).
Essential Fly-Fishing Knots and Leaders Principle 2: Traditional trout flies that float are called dry flies (p. 38).
Essential Fly-Fishing Knots and Leaders Principle 3: They aredesigned to imitate the adultforms of mayflies, caddis flies, and other insects that trout and other fish feed (p. 38).
Essential Fly-Fishing Knots and Leaders Principle 4: Anglers usedry flies to catch fish that arefeeding on surface-hatchinginsects (p. 38).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Essential Fly-Fishing Knots and Leaders): The dry flies are tied inpatterns to look like the specificspecies of insect (p. 38).
Step 2 (Essential Fly-Fishing Knots and Leaders): This is calledmatching the hatch, and itis one of the most importantprinciples in fishing (p. 38).
Step 3 (Essential Fly-Fishing Knots and Leaders): If you seefish feeding on a specific insectthen you should use a fly thatclosely imitates this food source (p. 38).
Step 4 (Essential Fly-Fishing Knots and Leaders): In addition to shape, color andmovement, the size of the fly isalso important when matching the hatch (p. 38).
